Despite soaring demand for GLP-1s, many eligible patients are unable to access these drugs for weight loss
In just a few short years, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have surged in popularity across the United States, transforming from specialized treatments for type 2 diabetes into revolutionary therapeutics for weight management, cardiovascular health and other emerging uses. But not all populations are benefiting from this expansion. As GLP-1 use has increased, disparities in access to these drugs have widened significantly, according to a new study led by researchers at Boston University School of Public Health (BUSPH).
Published in the journal Health Affairs Scholar, the study found that the percentage of patients with overweight or obesity and without type 2 diabetes who filled prescriptions for semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy) and tirzepatide (sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound) within six months of becoming eligible surged from 1.9% in 2021 to 16.6% in 2025.
But prescriptions for these medications were lower among men, Black or Hispanic patients, younger or older patients (ages 18–34 or 55–64), patients in a lower BMI category and/or patients whose health care provider was located in a neighborhood with lower socioeconomic status (SES), measured by education levels in the provider's ZIP code.
These disparities widened over time and were particularly pronounced in 2024 and 2025, after semaglutide and tirzepatide received formal approval by the Food and Drug Administration for chronic weight management in 2021 and 2023, respectively.
By mimicking a natural hormone that helps regulate insulin, blood sugar, appetite and digestion, GLP-1s can help people achieve dramatic weight loss, particularly those who struggle to lose weight through traditional diet and exercise. Health experts worry that persistent challenges with GLP-1 accessibility and affordability are hindering large swaths of eligible people from receiving life-changing and potentially lifesaving treatment.
"Our study focuses on a population that is especially vulnerable to inequities in GLP-1 access," says study senior author Dr. Andrew Stokes, an associate professor of global health at BUSPH, who studies population health, aging and mortality, including inequities in GLP-1 access.
"We have better treatments for obesity than ever, but access to them hasn't caught up. It is much easier for people with diabetes to get these drugs covered by insurance. But for people living with overweight or obesity, coverage is very difficult to obtain—even when they qualify—because providers and insurers don't always view these as conditions that merit treatment. This is a population that has been left behind."
As these medications continue to gain prominence, the findings underscore the need for health care providers to receive appropriate training and resources about prescribing GLP-1 treatments, as well as the need for improvements in insurance companies' drug benefit design to ensure that people who qualify for these treatments can easily access them.
"GLP-1 receptor agonists are moving into routine care very quickly, but without deliberate action, these drugs risk widening the health inequities that obesity already reflects," says study lead and corresponding author Dr. Minh Trung Le, a research data analyst in the Department of Global Health at BUSPH at the time of the study.
Stokes and Le utilized medical claims data from a national database that includes closed claims for more than 175 million patients. For the analysis, they examined health information, GLP-1 treatment and health care provider locations among 512,389 eligible, commercially insured patients ages 18–64. The analysis did not include patients covered by Medicaid or Medicare, people without insurance or prescriptions obtained through direct-to-consumer channels.
Despite the nearly ninefold rise in GLP-1 prescriptions among eligible patients during the study period, the researchers point out that the vast majority of eligible patients still do not receive these prescriptions for weight management. People with employer-sponsored and other commercial insurance are more likely to have access to GLP-1s.
That racial disparities in access to these medications were still evident among the study's commercially insured participants underscores the long-standing structural barriers to health care that Black and Hispanic patients experience, even as they are burdened by obesity and other health conditions at greater rates than other populations. Black and Hispanic patients are more likely to face biases and stigma in health care, mistrust of the health care system and higher medication costs, all of which can exacerbate racial disparities in GLP-1 uptake.
The expansion in GLP-1 medication use also disproportionately benefited patients who saw providers in higher-SES neighborhoods. These SES disparities were smaller in the beginning of the study period but widened over time and were larger among patients in lower BMI categories. These disparities were also particularly pronounced among men, which the researchers say may reflect men's lower likelihood of seeking weight-management care.
"Patients seen at clinics in lower socioeconomic neighborhoods had about 35% lower odds of being prescribed semaglutide or tirzepatide in 2024–2025; early on, that gap was about 15%," says Le. Insurance coverage alone doesn't close the gap, he says. "We need to look at how drug benefits are designed, including prior authorization, step therapy and out-of-pocket costs that land unevenly on different patients. We also need to give under-resourced practices real support, such as help with prior-authorization paperwork, so that a clinic's administrative capacity doesn't decide who gets treated."
"These important results show how emerging patterns of GLP-1 access reflect the inequity and fragmentation of our overall health care system, where access to affordable care is all too often a function of where you work, what state you live in or how much money you have," says Dr. Katherine Hempstead, who was not involved in the study and is a senior policy officer at the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation studying health issues and policies related to health insurance, costs and access to care.
Wealthier patients—many of whom may not clinically qualify for weight-management medications—are often able to leverage their network and resources to pay out of pocket for these medications, she adds. "The new direct-to-consumer channels for GLP-1s are increasing inequity, as ability to pay, rather than need or potential benefit, is what determines access. Because of the poor incentives and shortsightedness in our system, we are leaving major population health benefits on the table, since many of those who would benefit the most from these medications can't afford them."
The researchers say the findings add urgency to a growing shift in the health care field to view obesity as a chronic disease, rather than a personal responsibility or lifestyle failure.
"A doctor would never tell a patient with diabetes or with heart disease that their only option is to 'modify their dietary regimens' or 'exercise more,'" Stokes says. "When you think about obesity as a disease, it implies the value of effective medical treatment for the clinical factors that need to be addressed."
More information

candidato.titulo: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
candidato.resumo: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
- Date:
- November 21, 2026
- Source:
- Monash University
- Summary:
- The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

The human family tree may be due for a major rewrite. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional way scientists classify our ancient ancestors, suggesting that several groups long considered separate from humans may actually belong within our own genus, Homo.
The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution. Its central argument is that all human species and their closely related fossil relatives from the past 4 to 5 million years should be classified within the genus Homo.
That would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans. Although these ancient relatives differed considerably in appearance, anatomy, and behavior, the researchers argue that the evolutionary boundaries separating them are becoming increasingly difficult to justify.
Why the Human Family Tree May Need to Be Redrawn
Human evolution is frequently illustrated as a relatively orderly progression, beginning with ancestors that resembled apes and gradually moving through species such as Australopithecus and early Homo before arriving at modern humans, Homo sapiens.
However, evolution did not unfold as a simple sequence in which one species neatly replaced another. Instead, the fossil evidence reveals a complicated family tree with numerous branches, overlapping species, and evolutionary relationships that scientists are still working to understand.
Each new fossil discovery can complicate that picture. Traits once believed to distinguish one group of ancient human relatives from another have increasingly been found across multiple groups, making it harder to determine where traditional classifications should begin and end.
Dr. Ian Towle, a Research Fellow at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and lead researcher on the study, argues that these discoveries are exposing weaknesses in the existing classification system. This applies not only to species already assigned to Homo, but also to members of Australopithecus and Paranthropus, groups that lived during the past 5 million years.
"Recent fossil discoveries and advances in evolutionary and genetic analysis make this an ideal time to reconsider whether our traditional taxonomy still accurately reflects human evolution," Dr. Towle said.
"These groups do not necessarily represent distinct evolutionary branches, or 'clades', and differences in behavior and ecology once used to distinguish them have also become increasingly difficult to maintain.
"I propose expanding Homo to include these other groups to provide a more accurate and stable way to represent the complex evolutionary relationships revealed by the growing fossil record."
How Scientists Classify Our Ancient Ancestors
To understand the proposed change, it helps to look at how scientists organize living and extinct organisms.
The system is known as taxonomy, which involves naming species and arranging them into groups based on their characteristics and evolutionary relationships.
A genus is one level of this system, sitting above the species level. Modern humans, for example, belong to the species Homo sapiens, with Homo identifying our genus and sapiens identifying our species.
Over the past 50 years, advances in evolutionary research have significantly changed how scientists approach classification. Rather than relying primarily on physical similarities, modern taxonomy increasingly seeks to organize species according to their actual evolutionary ancestry.
An important concept in this approach is the clade. A clade consists of a common ancestor and all of its descendants. By grouping organisms this way, scientists aim to produce classifications that accurately reflect the branches of the evolutionary tree.
This approach has become increasingly influential in biology over recent decades. However, Towle argues that the classification of our own evolutionary relatives has been slower to adopt these principles consistently.
Why Brain Size and Tool Use No Longer Define Humans
Traditionally, scientists have distinguished members of the genus Homo from other ancient human relatives using a combination of physical and behavioral characteristics.
These have included relatively large brains, sophisticated tool use, and particular anatomical features associated with human evolution.
But discoveries over recent decades have challenged the reliability of those distinctions.
Scientists have identified members of Homo with surprisingly small brains, demonstrating that a large brain was not necessarily a defining characteristic of every species in our genus.
At the same time, evidence suggests that species traditionally placed in Australopithecus and Paranthropus likely displayed more complex behaviors than researchers once assumed.
Together, these findings have weakened the boundaries used to separate the three groups. Characteristics once thought to be exclusive to Homo may have been shared more widely among our ancient relatives.
As a result, determining which species belong within the human genus has become increasingly complicated. Towle argues that the problem may lie not with the fossil evidence, but with the classification system scientists are trying to fit it into.
A Radical Proposal for 5 Million Years of Human Evolution
Towle's proposed solution is to expand the genus Homo to include species currently classified as Australopithecus and Paranthropus.
The idea is not that these ancient relatives were identical to modern humans or possessed all the traits associated with our species. Rather, the broader classification would recognize their evolutionary connections while still allowing scientists to distinguish among individual species.
Such a change could also make human taxonomy more stable. Instead of repeatedly revising the boundaries between major groups whenever new fossils are uncovered, scientists could use a broader genus that accommodates the diversity revealed by ongoing discoveries.
The proposal represents a significant departure from traditional classifications, and it remains a scientific argument rather than an officially adopted change. Nevertheless, it highlights how much our understanding of human origins has evolved as new evidence has accumulated.
"The more we learn about our ancestors and close fossil relatives, the more we realize how complex and non-linear our family tree is," Dr. Towle said.
"Expanding the Homo genus to also include species of Australopithecus and Paranthropus will allow us to account for differences without regularly reclassifying particular groups."
Ultimately, the research raises a fundamental question about how scientists define the human family. If the traits once used to separate our ancestors are not as distinctive as previously believed, the names and categories used to describe millions of years of human evolution may need to change along with our understanding of the past.

candidato.titulo: How Google Traced GKE API Timeouts to a Linux Kernel TCP Bug
candidato.resumo: Google recently detailed how three interacting bugs across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, and the Linux kernel caused intermittent Kubernetes API connectivity failures, blocking around 800 developers from deploying to production. By Renato Losio

texto_fonte:
Google recently detailed how three interacting bugs across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, and the Linux kernel caused intermittent Kubernetes API connectivity failures, blocking around 800 developers from deploying to production.
In January, a customer running multiple GKE clusters with Private Service Connect (PSC) for private control-plane access experienced intermittent timeouts when pods attempted to reach the Kubernetes API server.
Packet captures revealed that the control plane was responding to new TCP connection requests with stale ACK packets belonging to previously closed connections. The root cause involved three separate bugs across different networking layers. Akash Thakur, senior technical solutions engineer at Google Cloud, describes how engineers across multiple Google teams identified three root causes and ultimately addressed them:
In a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself.
The investigation identified three interacting causes: packet reordering in PSC, Envoy's half-close behavior preventing TCP connections from being properly closed, and a Linux kernel bug that discarded certain reordered FIN packets.
Source: Google Cloud blog
Thakur describes a complex troubleshooting case involving I/O timeouts across Private Service Connect, virtual network interfaces, and the Linux TCP state machine, which ultimately revealed a kernel issue leaving sockets stuck indefinitely in the FIN_WAIT_2 state.  Thakur explains:
Most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete.
The issue was addressed through three coordinated fixes over several weeks: Google first rolled back a Private Service Connect change to restore connectivity, then corrected the proxy protocol handling and added regression tests. Finally, a Linux kernel patch, authored by Eric Dumazet, formerly a software engineer at Google, fixed the underlying TCP issue. Rohan Karne, managing director at Google Cloud, comments:
This is the unglamorous reality of mission-critical platform engineering—methodically ruling out the obvious suspects and digging into packet captures until you find the kernel root cause.
Thakur highlights how individually reasonable behaviors across networking, proxies and operating systems can combine into complex infrastructure failures. Packet captures at multiple network layers were essential to identifying the problem, while correlating network symptoms with infrastructure changes helped establish the connection between the three bugs. Guangba Yu, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, highlights:
For AIOps and chaos engineering, the transferable method is organizing simultaneous path observations, protocol state, and rollout events while distinguishing symptom recovery from state-machine correction. This anonymized case supplies no population failure rate and does not explain all API timeouts.
Justin Garrison, field CTO at Sidero, notes:
At first I was excited to read this article that leads to a kernel patch which are always fun. It turns out GKE just runs a kernel from 3 years ago (6.1) and the bug was already fixed upstream and they had to backport it.
The kernel fix was merged into Linux 6.9.7 and backported to the 6.6 and 6.1 LTS branches, reaching GKE customers in version 1.33.5 and later.

candidato.titulo: This week on Tom's Hardware Premium: 21 November 2026
candidato.resumo: We go through an exhaustive list of everything we covered at SC26, which includes brand-new devices and developments from AMD, Nvidia, Intel and many more.

texto_fonte:
In case you're worried about missing out on all the goodness on Tom's Hardware Premium, we've rounded up everything that we've published this week right here. The main theme for this week has been coverage straight from the show floor at the annual Supercomputing conference (SC26). If you've not yet caught up, you've been missing out, as all of our coverage from the conference is currently free to access. All you need to do is sign up or log in to your Tom's Hardware account to enjoy all of our coverage from the show.
First up, our resident CPU boffin, Jake Roach, has been on the show floor all week, offering us a direct line to all the goings-on at the conference, including an interesting back-and-forth from Nvidia and AMD on their CPUs. AMD claims that its latest EPYC Venice lineup is the best at agentic workloads, while Nvidia's marketing material characterized Nvidia's Vera CPU as being purpose-built for Agentic AI. At SC26, Nvidia CPU chief Ian Finder rebuked Nvidia's own marketing material, stating that the idea that Nvidia could have predicted the Data Center moment was "absurd," instead saying that the company's design know-how helped them develop the processor.
In this interview, we sit down with Finder to find out how Vera came to be, what agentic workloads mean for the CPU industry, and where Nvidia's headed next.
Nvidia's Vera CPU was a hot topic at SC26, as the company explained that existing software cannot always take full advantage of the processor without architecture-specific optimization. The company showed that under some workloads, Vera's performance can be optimized by up to 39% when taking its Olympus-based Arm cores into account. However, it remains to be seen how much performance can be gained from Olympus-specific hardware optimization workloads other than matrix multiplication.
Nvidia also announced a Rubin GPU variant, named Rubin HPC, a chip that the company claims is purpose-built for agentic workflows and scientific simulations that demand processing large datasets. While technical details remain scant, Nvidia says that Rubin HPC sports over 50,000 CUDA cores, or slightly below double the number of cores present in the standard-issue Rubin GPU. We explored all the details and possibilities that the newly announced chip might offer.
AMD is now featured in over 40% of the new TOP500 list of supercomputers, with a 14% boost to the company's position. Leading the company is Lux, a supercomputer developed in conjunction with the U.S. Department of Energy. The second supercomputer, Discovery, is expected to debut in 2028, sporting a suite of EPYC CPUs and Instinct accelerators.
Within the TOP500, not much has changed... at the top, with the top 10 systems remaining unchanged, as China's LineShine system in Shenzhen remains at the top of the list, with El Capitan remaining second. We take a look at the entire list and how the focus has seemingly shifted toward AI compute capacity. While the demand for HPC hardware is at an all-time high, it appears as though the vast majority of that hardware isn't being tested against the TOP500 benchmark.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
- AMD grabs over 40% of new TOP500 list for supercomputers, up 14% since last year — new Lux system developed between AMD and Department of Energy debuts at no. 14 with EPYC CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPUs
- China retains fastest supercomputer in the world crown as AI data centers soak up new hardware — Top500 records fewest new systems in 33 years
Despite AI clusters seemingly eating up compute capacity, AMD recognizes that the burgeoning segment will never wholly replace HPC computing, and that high-precision workloads will continue to be necessary. AMD's Scott Tease further suggested that building a heterogeneous compute stack would be the best path forward for tackling complex research problems. This point dovetails nicely into how AMD additionally touted that its MI430X's native FP64 operations will beat out emulated support for the full-precision data types seen in Nvidia's hardware. This is notable, as the company claims that Ozaki FP64 emulation could have cascading effects on memory usage, which is in notorious levels of undersupply.
- Researchers ‘recognize that AI will never replace HPC,’ says AMD executive — high-precision workloads will ‘exist for a very long time’ even as AI usage expands
- AMD attacks Nvidia's FP64 emulation at SC26, touts native double-precision on Instinct MI430X — says Ozaki schemes fit less than 10% of HPC workloads and triple memory use and emulated FP64 is a poor fit for many HPC workloads
Not wanting to be left out of the conversation, Intel's next-generation Diamond Rapids CPUs surfaced at SC26, but not from Intel itself, curiously. On the ground, we saw the chips turn up at the CXL booth and at Bull, where the CPU was shown installed in a server. While there were no demos available, the company did show off demos for Xeon 6+ and its Crescent Island GPU.
Elsewhere at the show, PCI 6 devices and controllers have started to surface. First, Silicon Motion's SM8466 controller was demoed at the show, armed with PerformaShape 2, which increases the number of quality-of-service sets from 256 to 512, alongside additional boons.
Elsewhere, Phison detailed two new enterprise SSDs: one that comes with a built-in NPU and 64GB of memory, and another that is set to merge pSLC cache, with high QLC capacity on a single controller. We explore what makes these devices notable and why, though the company itself notes that the devices are very much still in development.
- Silicon Motion demos SM8466 PCIe 6.0 SSD controller, expected to ship by 2028 — controller boasts improved quality of service, samples imminent
- Phison details SSD with a built-in NPU and 64GB of 130 GB/s memory to run PyTorch and llama.cpp on-drive — claims up to 100x less data transfer alongside new mixed media pSLC and QLC design
VAST Data explained how petabyte-scale SSDs will outgrow the tried and true RAID parallel filesystems, according to a simulation the company ran on its own 900 PB system, which puts the odds of data loss at a staggering 1 in 11 over a decade. We explain all in detail about how it works.
As enterprise hardware and the titanic growth of AI superclusters push the limits of our existing material infrastructure, from interconnects to grid energy and raw materials, researchers from The Ohio State University discussed how high-performance networking could soon scale across entire regions. We explore how faster networking connections could spell a future where distributed computing systems communicate across vast distances.

candidato.resumo: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

texto_fonte:
A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
- Date:
- November 21, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.
- Share:
Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a new lease on life.
Researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.
Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.
"Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing."
How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion
For thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.
Once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly quickly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.
The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.
"We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!"
Scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.
"When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space."
A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome
This kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.
As the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.
For Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.
But such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.
These surviving systems are important because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.
Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.
Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb
To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.
The telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.
The simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.
Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Big Bao."
"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.
The researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.
At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.
Further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Big Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.
Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De said.
The merger has left astronomers with another important question: What is Bao like now?
The surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.
Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs
One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.
Although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.
The researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.)
The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.
Earlier records showed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.
By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) showed further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.
Another important development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.
The telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.
Then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.
Scientists quickly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable new measurements.
Webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.
A New Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars
The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an important advance in the study of stellar mergers.
Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.
That timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.
The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.
NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.
One of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.
With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.
"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar said.
The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.
The James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever launched, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.
Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

candidato.titulo: A tiny superconducting sandwich could help computers use less energy
candidato.resumo: MIT researchers combined superconducting and magnetic layers in a tiny device offering persistent memory and signal control for more energy-efficient computing.

texto_fonte:
Scientists at the MIT Plasma Science and Fusion Center (PSFC) have created a tiny superconducting device that could help future computers store and process information using far less energy.
Today’s computers, supercomputers, and data centers need more of everything to keep up with demand: more energy, more capacity, and more speed to perform increasingly complex tasks. Feeding those computers’ processors with information — fast — is part of the challenge.
That’s where random access memory, or RAM, comes in. It’s a computer’s working space, keeping the information needed for current tasks close at hand. Without enough RAM, a computer slows down as it repeatedly retrieves information from hard drives or other longer-term storage.
Most familiar RAM is volatile: Turn off the power, and its contents disappear. There’s also nonvolatile memory, like the kind in a flash drive, which retains information without power. But there are trade-offs. Flash memory, for example, is slower to write than conventional RAM, and repeated writing and erasing eventually wear it out. Other forms of nonvolatile memory have different strengths and limitations.
In an effort to create faster, more energy-efficient computers, researchers have been developing superconducting computers, which rely on superconductors — a material that, when cold enough, exhibits no electrical resistance — instead of the traditional semiconductors to write information. In theory, the switch to superconductors allows for much quicker information processing with less heat emitted. But, processing is only as good as the memory that can supply those processors. It’s been a challenge to develop fast, high-capacity memory that also works at the extremely cold temperatures needed to operate superconducting computers.
Researchers at the PSFC have made a device that could help. In their recently published Physics Review Letters paper, titled “Magnetic Exchange-Coupled Superconducting Devices with Broken Symmetry for Cryogenic Memory,” senior research scientist Jagadeesh Moodera and his colleagues, including first author and postdoc Josep Ingla-Aynés, describe the device, which is a tiny sandwich made of an ultrathin superconducting film between two magnetic layers that can act as a memory cell. The magnets determine whether the film’s superconductivity is switched on or off.
"Integrating these devices can lead to processors operating at high speed and low energy,” says Moodera. “This development addresses the current lack of suitable cryogenic memory and control components, allowing for the advancement of cryogenic electronics technologies, including quantum computing and networking."
At the memory cell’s operating temperature, depending on whether a current can pass through or not, a computer can distinguish between two states and read them as a 0 or a 1, which is a bit, the smallest unit of data in a computer.
Writing a bit means, in this case, changing the magnetic alignment in the memory cell’s film: If the magnetization is pointing in opposite directions, the current can pass through; if it’s the same direction, the film becomes resistive. The researchers change the magnetic alignment by applying a small magnetic field and an electrical pulse that briefly heats the selected cell, making its magnetization easier to switch. Once set, the magnetic alignment stays in place without a continuing pulse or applied field. Each cell remembers. Moreover, it takes less energy to change that magnetic alignment in these cells and encode the bit than it does in traditional semiconductor cells.
The device still needs to stay extremely cold to operate, but each bit does not need a continuous electrical supply to preserve its state — it’s nonvolatile memory.
The researchers demonstrated that they could switch one cell without changing a neighboring cell, which is key when building memory in which individual bits can be selected and rewritten. The thought is that smaller cells could allow more information to fit into a compact space and could reduce the time and energy needed to write it.
According to Ingla-Aynés, “Any useful memory must have the ability to change one bit without disturbing all the information around it. Showing that we could switch a single cell without losing the neighbor's memory state was an important step toward bringing this superconducting layered device closer to a practical memory technology.”
The sandwich has another useful trick: It can also control where electrical signals go.
At a lower temperature, the device acts as a superconducting diode, which is like an on/off switch for delivering electricity in a certain direction. Within a particular range of currents, the device lets current flow without resistance in one direction while presenting resistance in the other. Changing the magnetic alignment can reverse that preferred direction, or create a resistive “off” state. Those settings could be used to direct or block the electrical pulses that carry information through superconducting circuits.
Having both capabilities in the same layered structure opens possibilities for combining memory and signal control on a superconducting chip. With that technology, superconducting computers could become a practical, energy-efficient alternative to the traditional computers currently relied upon for energy-intensive applications like AI. Moreover, while the devices store regular bits rather than quantum computers’ qubits, both quantum and traditional computers need reliable ways to hold information and move signals; the devices could potentially provide memory and signal control for quantum computers’ supporting electronics. Placing these devices near the cryogenic systems needed for superconducting operation could help reduce heat and electromagnetic interference that can disrupt the qubits’ fragile quantum state.
The researchers have demonstrated that their device can be used as an individually switchable, nonvolatile memory cell that could potentially serve as a building block for a new generation of highly efficient computers. The next challenge is to make these devices smaller and combine them into arrays capable of storing large amounts of information, while also quantifying just how much energy savings is possible in a system comprised of these devices.

candidato.resumo: A PC cooling enthusiast attached a bounce house blower to the bottom of his laptop, bringing temperatures below 50 degrees Celsius.

texto_fonte:
Experimental PC modder Trash Bench recently tested a laptop cooler and tried to beat it with increasingly powerful blower setups, eventually opting for a bounce house inflator blower to cool the i7-10750H and RTX 2070 MaxQ with a 90W power limit. He was able to bring temperatures down from 84 degrees Celsius to 48.8 degrees Celsius, with Cyberpunk going from 47 FPS to 56 FPS.
Trash Bench was asked to review a laptop cooling stand, but he said he doesn’t do reviews, so he proposed a video idea: He’ll test the laptop cooler and try to beat it with his creations—no opening the laptop, no sub-ambient cooling solutions, only airflow.
The Llano V12 laptop cooling fan sent to Trash Bench achieved an impressive 58.3 degrees Celsius average on the GPU at medium settings, dropping 27 degrees from the stock 84 degrees Celsius. The lower temperatures also improved gaming performance by an average of 19.4%. Pushing the Llano V12 to 100% made it incredibly loud, but it only reached 56.7 degrees Celsius with negligible performance gains.
His first attempt to beat the Llano V12 was using the Noctua NF-A20, a huge 200mm fan, and a 3D-printed duct with foam around the edges, like the Llano V12, to prevent air leaks. Unfortunately, the single 200mm fan didn't beat the Llano V12, with GPU temperatures averaging 66.3 degrees Celsius—still pretty impressive given the setup's simplicity, if you ignore the messy PC power supply and fan speed controller beside it.
His second attempt used six Arctic P12 fans at full speed, beating the Llano V12 by 0.9 degrees Celsius at medium settings and achieving an average GPU temperature of 57.4 degrees Celsius. However, it lost to the full-speed Llano V12, but only barely. The third attempt used two 4000 RPM server fans, which were even louder than the six full-speed Arctic P12S — but that finally did the trick, beating the Llano V12 at 100% by 2.6 degrees Celsius.

And just to go extreme, like Trash Bench often does in his experiments, he used a powerful blower fan designed to inflate bounce houses. He took advantage of the larger foam gaskets the Llano V12 used and 3D-printed an interface at the bottom of the laptop cooler’s housing to fit a flexible duct. The sheer force of the air lifted the laptop off the stand, so it needed to be taped down to seal the air leak.
The bounce house blower produced an average GPU temperature of 48.8 degrees Celsius, but saw very little performance gain over the Llano V12 at 100%, six Arctic P12s, and the pair of server fans, with Time Spy benchmark results within 1% of each other. The Noctua was the weakest in the benchmarks, however, lagging by 3% behind the bounce house blower, but was much quieter.

texto_fonte:
Governança de IA: 5 que falhas podem comprometer adoção da tecnologia em empresas
Por Rodrigo Resende |
A inteligência artificial já faz parte da rotina de muitas empresas, mas incorporar a tecnologia às operações é apenas uma etapa do processo. À medida que novas ferramentas e agentes passam a executar atividades, acessar informações e apoiar decisões, cresce também a necessidade de estabelecer critérios para orientar e controlar seu uso. Nesse cenário, a governança de IA deixa de ser uma preocupação restrita à área de tecnologia e passa a ser um elemento fundamental para garantir que a adoção aconteça de forma segura, coordenada e alinhada aos objetivos do negócio.
Quando diferentes departamentos adotam soluções de IA sem critérios compartilhados, o que deveria representar um ganho de produtividade pode gerar problemas operacionais, riscos de segurança e custos difíceis de administrar. O desafio não está apenas em incorporar novas ferramentas, mas em entender como elas serão utilizadas, por quem e com qual finalidade.
Um levantamento do Capgemini Research Institute, publicado em 2025 e realizado com 1.100 executivos de grandes empresas de 15 países, ajuda a dimensionar essa questão. Embora 93% das organizações pesquisadas já explorassem, testassem ou implementassem recursos de inteligência artificial generativa, apenas 46% possuíam políticas de governança estabelecidas. Entre aquelas que contavam com essas diretrizes, 47% relataram que seus funcionários raramente as seguiam. Os dados mostram que o interesse e a implementação da tecnologia nem sempre são acompanhados pela maturidade necessária para administrá-la.
Na prática, cinco erros podem comprometer os resultados dessa transformação:
1. Acreditar que quanto mais IA, melhor
Um dos equívocos na adoção de novas tecnologias é associar o avanço tecnológico à quantidade de ferramentas disponíveis.
Na tentativa de acompanhar o mercado, algumas empresas passam a incorporar soluções de inteligência artificial até mesmo em atividades nas quais a tecnologia não oferece vantagens claras ou um processo mais simples já resolveria o problema.
Nem toda tarefa precisa de IA. Antes de implementar uma solução, é importante identificar qual problema ela deve resolver, quais resultados são esperados e se existe uma alternativa mais adequada.
Sem essa avaliação, a organização corre o risco de acumular ferramentas, aumentar a complexidade da operação e investir recursos em aplicações que pouco contribuem para o negócio.
Essa análise também deve considerar a qualidade dos resultados. Uma ferramenta pode automatizar determinada atividade, mas exigir tantas revisões e correções humanas que o ganho de produtividade acaba sendo reduzido ou até anulado.
2. Permitir que cada área utilize ferramentas sem critérios comuns
Quando cada departamento escolhe suas próprias soluções, sem alinhamento com as diretrizes da empresa, surgem diferentes ambientes de utilização da IA.
Uma equipe pode contratar uma plataforma, outra desenvolver uma aplicação independente e uma terceira compartilhar informações corporativas em ferramentas externas sem que a área de tecnologia tenha conhecimento.
Esse cenário dificulta o controle sobre quais sistemas estão sendo utilizados, quais dados são compartilhados e quem tem acesso a eles. Também pode criar dependência de fornecedores e soluções que não se comunicam entre si.
Por isso, é fundamental estabelecer regras claras de utilização, definir quais ferramentas são autorizadas e orientar os colaboradores sobre os limites de uso. Um primeiro passo é fazer um levantamento das soluções de IA utilizadas pelos diferentes departamentos, identificando suas finalidades, os responsáveis por cada aplicação e os tipos de dados envolvidos.
A governança precisa alcançar toda a organização, sem ficar restrita à equipe de tecnologia.
3. Multiplicar agentes de IA sem coordenar suas atividades
Com a evolução da tecnologia, os agentes de IA passaram a executar tarefas que antes exigiam a participação humana em diferentes etapas de um processo. O desafio aparece quando as empresas começam a criar múltiplos agentes sem definir claramente o papel e os limites de atuação de cada um.
Imagine uma operação em que dois agentes recebem responsabilidades semelhantes, processam informações diferentes ou executam instruções conflitantes.
Um agente encarregado de atualizar registros de clientes, por exemplo, pode modificar informações utilizadas simultaneamente por outro sistema para gerar relatórios ou tomar decisões. Se não houver mecanismos de coordenação e verificação, uma alteração incorreta poderá comprometer outras etapas do trabalho.
Em vez de agilizar a operação, esses conflitos podem gerar retrabalho, decisões contraditórias e novas necessidades de verificação. Em fluxos mais complexos, um agente pode até desfazer ou comprometer uma ação realizada por outro.
A adoção desses sistemas exige planejamento. É preciso determinar quais atividades cada agente pode executar, quais informações pode acessar, como deve interagir com outros sistemas e em quais situações uma decisão precisa passar pela validação humana.
Também é importante manter registros das ações executadas, testar o comportamento dos agentes e limitar suas permissões às atividades realmente necessárias. Dessa forma, a empresa consegue identificar falhas, investigar decisões e reduzir os riscos associados à autonomia desses sistemas.
4. Ignorar o impacto financeiro do uso da IA
Outro erro é considerar apenas o custo inicial de contratação de uma ferramenta, sem acompanhar o que acontece depois que ela passa a fazer parte da operação.
O uso de inteligência artificial depende de recursos de processamento, infraestrutura e energia, cujos custos podem ser cobrados diretamente pelo consumo ou estar incorporados ao preço dos serviços contratados. Dependendo da solução, da frequência de utilização e da complexidade das tarefas, as despesas podem crescer significativamente.
Quando há ferramentas redundantes, agentes executando atividades desnecessárias e processos mal dimensionados, a conta pode se tornar ainda mais elevada. Em plataformas que cobram por volume de processamento ou de informações utilizadas, por exemplo, tarefas repetidas e chamadas desnecessárias aos modelos podem aumentar os gastos sem produzir resultados adicionais.
Uma pesquisa divulgada pela IBM em junho de 2026 identificou que 84% dos executivos de tecnologia entrevistados ainda não haviam operacionalizado completamente a gestão financeira da IA, enquanto 85% não tinham visibilidade integral dos gastos com a tecnologia em tempo real.
Isso reforça a importância de acompanhar o consumo e relacionar os custos aos resultados entregues. Indicadores como custo por tarefa, tempo economizado e redução de erros podem ajudar a verificar se o investimento realmente compensa.
A tecnologia precisa gerar valor mensurável. Caso contrário, a empresa pode ampliar seus investimentos sem perceber que parte dos recursos está sendo desperdiçada.
5. Deixar a segurança dos dados em segundo plano
A facilidade de acesso às ferramentas de IA também exige atenção ao tipo de informação que circula por elas. Funcionários podem inserir dados de clientes, documentos internos, informações financeiras ou conteúdos estratégicos em plataformas sem compreender como esses materiais serão armazenados e utilizados.
O risco não está apenas em ataques externos. A própria ausência de regras e controles pode levar ao compartilhamento indevido de informações e à exposição de dados que deveriam permanecer restritos.
Uma situação aparentemente simples, como utilizar uma ferramenta pública de IA para resumir um contrato confidencial ou analisar uma planilha com dados de clientes, pode representar um risco caso a empresa não tenha avaliado as condições de armazenamento, processamento e utilização dessas informações pelo fornecedor.
As empresas precisam definir níveis de acesso, estabelecer quais informações podem ser utilizadas em cada ferramenta e criar mecanismos de acompanhamento. Também é importante preparar os colaboradores para reconhecer situações em que o uso da IA exige cautela ou autorização prévia.
Esses cuidados devem incluir a avaliação das políticas de privacidade e segurança dos fornecedores, a classificação das informações corporativas e a revisão periódica das permissões concedidas aos sistemas.
Governar para conseguir avançar
Esses cinco erros têm um ponto em comum: mostram que a adoção da inteligência artificial não pode acontecer de maneira isolada, sem considerar o funcionamento da organização como um todo.
A governança precisa fazer parte da estratégia desde o início. Isso envolve mapear as ferramentas utilizadas, estabelecer responsabilidades, definir limites de atuação, acompanhar custos e revisar continuamente os processos. Também exige integração entre tecnologia, segurança da informação e áreas de negócio, já que os impactos da IA ultrapassam os limites de um único departamento.
Para empresas que ainda não possuem uma estrutura de governança, o primeiro passo pode ser identificar quais ferramentas já estão em uso, quais informações elas acessam e quem responde por suas operações. A partir desse diagnóstico, torna-se possível estabelecer prioridades, corrigir vulnerabilidades e definir critérios para novas implementações.
O potencial da inteligência artificial é enorme, mas sua adoção sem planejamento pode criar problemas que anulam parte dos ganhos esperados. O objetivo não deve ser utilizar IA em todas as atividades, mas identificar onde ela realmente faz sentido e garantir que seu uso esteja alinhado às necessidades e à capacidade operacional da empresa.

candidato.titulo: The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury
candidato.resumo: After an eight-year voyage towards the sun, the BepiColombo spacecraft can finally begin its mission to unpick the many mysteries of our solar system's smallest planet

texto_fonte:
After a long and ponderous journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft will finally enter Mercury’s orbit on 21 November. Over the course of the next year, it will investigate the planet’s geology, its tenuous atmosphere and its magnetic field in an effort to understand how it formed and evolved over time.
BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), launched in October 2018. Mercury’s proximity to the sun makes it incredibly difficult to reach without overshooting the planet and falling into the sun, so the spacecraft had to take a long and looping path over the past eight years, flying past both Venus and Mercury several times and using their gravity to make subtle tweaks to its trajectory. In 2024, an issue with the thrusters lengthened that journey even further, pushing the arrival date back from 2025 to 2026. Now, it has finally arrived.
While it is arriving at Mercury as a single spacecraft, BepiColombo actually comprises two separate orbiters: ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO, or Mio). In December, the two will split apart and move to different orbits – MPO on a near-circular path that takes 2.3 hours to complete an orbit, and Mio on a more distant elliptical orbit, where it will take 9.3 hours to circle Mercury.
Advertisement
Those split orbits complement the differing scientific objectives of the two spacecraft. MPO is more than twice the size of MMO, and its 11 scientific instruments focus largely on studying Mercury itself. Its instruments include several types of spectrometer to measure the makeup of the surface, a laser altimeter to map its terrain and instruments to study the makeup of Mercury’s extremely thin atmosphere, called an exosphere.
Mio’s more distant orbit will allow it to study a broader area around Mercury. It has five sets of scientific instruments to study the magnetic field and atmosphere of the planet, as well as the solar wind that blows strongly in the area close to the sun.
Now that the BepiColombo spacecraft are entering orbit, their primary mission is expected to last only one Earth year, which is a little more than four Mercury years. The mission could potentially be extended for another year, but beyond that the combination of limited fuel and extreme temperatures will make it all but impossible to keep going.
Over the course of the year, researchers hope that BepiColombo will provide enough data to solve some of Mercury’s many mysteries. Mercury’s magnetic field is bewildering, because it originates 400 kilometres above the planet’s centre and should have faded away long ago. Its atmosphere must be continuously supplied with material from the surface, but we are unsure exactly how that occurs. And its enormous iron core, much bigger proportionally than the core of any other planet in the solar system, makes its very formation and evolution a puzzle. If all goes well, BepiColombo will start to unravel the convoluted tale of our solar system’s smallest planet.

candidato.titulo: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
candidato.resumo: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use "advanced cryptographic tools" to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

texto_fonte:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”
But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].
The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.
The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.
The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.
Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.
A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.
But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.
“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”
Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.
In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.
“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”
The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.
“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”
Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.
“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”
The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.
Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
